column2: To look after only one's own interest in every matter.
column3: To hew toward oneself like a clog-maker's adze.
column4: The nalıncı was the craftsman who made the wooden clogs (nalın) worn in bathhouses. The adze he used has a short handle and a blade that faces its user, so the clog-maker always hews the wood toward himself. This motion came to stand for a person who pulls every advantage toward himself. The idiom arose when Ottoman bathhouse culture was widespread and is said today of selfish people. Keser 'adze' derives from the Turkish root kesmek 'to cut'.

column2: For one's poor quality or hidden flaw to be exposed.
column3: For the thread of one's weaving to become visible at the market.
column4: In weaving, the thread of poor-quality cloth shows through after repeated washing; when customers saw this at the market, the weaver's name was ruined. Guild inspectors also checked the thread count of cloth and publicly displayed defective pieces in the marketplace. The idiom arose from this market inspection and describes a person's hidden flaws becoming known to all. Today someone whose 'thread has gone to market' is an untrustworthy person.

column2: Of low quality; an unreliable person or thing.
column3: Of debased gold fineness.
column4: Ayar, of Arabic origin, denotes the degree of purity of gold; goldsmiths and the mint assessed every coin by its fineness. A coin whose ayar was 'spoiled' was counterfeit money alloyed with copper. Striking debased coin was a serious crime in the Ottoman state. The idiom was taken from this language of goldsmiths and the mint and applied to untrustworthy people. The form ayarı bozulmak has the same meaning.

column2: A criterion that serves to measure the value of something.
column3: The stone used to test the fineness of gold.
column4: Mihenk, of Arabic origin, is the black stone on which goldsmiths rubbed gold to test its fineness; the color of the streak left by the gold shows its purity. This touchstone was a basic tool in the Ottoman mint and the goldsmiths' bazaar. Starting from this concrete measuring instrument, the expression came to denote any criterion of value. Today it is used for the standard against which a person or an idea is tested.

column2: To put into writing; to write.
column3: To take in hand with a pen.
column4: Kalem, of Greek origin and borrowed into Turkish via Arabic, is a writing instrument made from reed. In calligraphers' workshops and the state chanceries every document was written with a reed pen, which is why kalem also became the name of a government office. The idiom describes committing a thought to paper with a pen. It comes from the same workshop as idioms such as kalem oynatmak 'to wield the pen' and kalem kırmak 'to break the pen'.

column2: One cannot find the time or will to do for oneself the work one does for others.
column3: The tailor cannot find time to mend the tear in his own clothes.
column4: Terzi, of Persian origin, is the craftsman who sews garments. A tailor who sews garments for his customers with great care has no time to mend his own torn seam. The proverb presents this observation as a rule of human nature: the service rendered to others is not applied to oneself. The saying arose from the language of the bazaar and is used today by analogy for every profession, such as doctors and barbers.

column2: A difficulty can only be removed by a similar difficulty.
column3: A driven nail is pulled out with another nail.
column4: In the carpenter's workshop a stuck nail is loosened and removed by driving a second nail beside it. Çivi 'nail' is a word in use since Old Turkic. The proverb turns this workshop knowledge into a principle of life: the cure for a trouble is found in a similar trouble. The same observation has become a proverb in other languages too. In Turkish it is said especially of a love that one wishes to forget.

column2: To say exactly the right thing at the right moment, with telling effect.
column3: To fit the stone exactly into the gap in the wall.
column4: A master mason dresses stones so that they fit exactly into the gedik, the gap in a wall; a well-set stone strengthens the wall. Gedik, meaning 'opening', derives from the Turkish root ged-. The idiom likens this feat of craftsmanship to a well-aimed remark. Today it is used for a pointed comment that silences the other side in a debate.

column2: To say something hurtful or do something wrong without realizing it.
column3: To bring the axe down on stone instead of wood.
column4: Woodcutters and carpenters bring the axe down on wood; an axe that mistakenly strikes stone is blunted, and the sound startles everyone. Balta 'axe' is a word in use since Old Turkic. The idiom likens this picture of clumsiness to an unintended gaffe. The saying is recorded in nineteenth-century dictionaries and today describes saying the wrong thing to the wrong person in conversation.

column2: Judge yourself more harshly before criticizing others.
column3: First stick the needle into yourself, then the packing needle into others.
column4: The çuvaldız is the thick, large needle used for sewing sacks; it hurts far more than an ordinary needle. The proverb advises that the measure one would apply to others should first be applied to oneself. Built from the tools of the tailor's and the sack-maker's workshop, the saying has lived on in oral tradition. Today it is said to convey that self-criticism should precede criticism of others.

column2: To conduct secret, underhanded dealings without anyone noticing.
column3: To run water beneath a pile of straw.
column4: On the threshing floor the straw of the threshed grain is left in large heaps; when water is channeled through a small ditch dug beneath such a heap, nothing is visible from above. In Anatolian villages the right to water was assigned by turn, and someone secretly drawing water to his field out of turn was a frequent cause of quarrels. The idiom arose from the image of such covert water theft and in time came to be used for every kind of sly undertaking.

column2: Thoroughly, completely, from the core to the very end.
column3: Right down to the tip of the stalk.
column4: When grain is cut with a sickle, cutting the ear right down to the base of the stalk means nothing is left in the field; in village speech this signals that the job has been done completely. A knife or dagger plunged in up to its hilt (sap) carries the same idea of completeness. Today the idiom is mostly used to stress that a quality is present in full: sapına kadar dürüst 'honest to the core', sapına kadar Anadolulu 'Anatolian through and through'.

column2: A place that is very messy, turned upside down and covered in dust.
column3: Like a threshing floor.
column4: The threshing floor is the open area where grain is driven over with a threshing sledge and the stalk is separated from chaff and kernel. At the end of threshing the place is covered with bits of straw, dust and scattered heaps, and animals and people have been moving about it all day. Starting from the sight of such a disordered space, the idiom is used to describe an untidy house or room.

column2: For a latecomer to try to oust the rightful owner.
column3: For someone who comes down from the mountain to drive out the one in the vineyard.
column4: The tension over land between the settled vine-grower and the nomad or stranger coming down from the mountains was a reality of Anatolian history for centuries. A vineyard is property that demands years of labor and is raised through grafting and pruning, while the newcomer from the mountain has invested no labor there. Born of this contrast, the idiom came to describe those who unjustly covet another's place.

column1: Dimyat'a pirince giderken evdeki bulgurdan olmak
column2: To lose what one already has while trying to obtain something better.
column3: To lose the bulgur at home while going to Damietta for rice.
column4: Dimyat (Damietta), in the Nile delta, was Egypt's principal rice-producing port city, exporting to the Mediterranean; in the Ottoman period Istanbul's rice came largely from there. Bulgur, by contrast, is the cheap and durable staple that Anatolia produced from its own wheat. Through an image drawn from Ottoman trade geography, the proverb describes chasing distant and expensive rice and losing the safe bulgur.

column2: To expect everything to come ready-made without any effort.
column3: Pear, ripen and fall into my mouth.
column4: A pear ripening in the sun falls from the branch on its own when its time comes, but for it to fall straight into someone's mouth is the lazy person's dream. In orchard culture, picking, drying and storing fruit requires labor; the idiom mocks the expectation that disregards this labor. Similar sayings were formed in Anatolia with other fruits, but the version with the pear became widespread.

column2: Small savings accumulate over time into something of great value.
column3: Drop by drop, a lake forms.
column4: In Anatolia, where rainfall is scarce, wells, cisterns and dams were the means of collecting water drop by drop; villagers channeled rainwater from their roofs into cisterns to get through the dry months. The proverb is the plainest expression of this thrift. A similar saying appears in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk, showing that patient accumulation was counseled among the early Turks as well.

column1: tarlada izi olmayanın harmanda yüzü olmaz
column2: Whoever has not contributed labor has no right to claim a share of the produce.
column3: Whoever has left no footprint in the field has no face at the threshing floor.
column4: In the seasons of sowing, hoeing and reaping, everyone who worked in the field left footprints in the soil; when the crop was divided at threshing time this labor was taken into account. In the imece system of communal labor, for someone who had not worked to come to the threshing floor and demand a share was considered shameful. The proverb sums up this village custom and ties entitlement to labor.

column2: To bear the good or bad consequences of what one has done.
column3: To reap what one has sown in the field.
column4: Whatever seed is sown, that is the crop reaped; a field sown with wheat does not yield barley. This plain agricultural truth has turned into a moral lesson in almost every language; the Kutadgu Bilig too says that whoever sows goodness reaps goodness. In Turkish the idiom is mostly used for negative outcomes: whoever sows evil reaps evil.

column2: To ruin a venture that was going well with a single mistake.
column3: To spoil a whole sackful of figs.
column4: Dried figs were the Aegean's most valuable export and were shipped packed in sacks; a single rotten or wormy fig that got into the sack could spoil the whole load. Merchants therefore inspected the figs one by one. The idiom carried this commercial reality over to the sense of a single error ruining an entire undertaking.

column2: To come under someone's oppression or domination.
column3: To go under the yoke.
column4: The boyunduruk is the wooden bar placed over the necks of the two oxen that pull a plow or an oxcart; once harnessed to the yoke, the animal can no longer move by its own will. The word boyunduruk is recorded in this sense in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk. The idiom transferred the condition of the plowing animal to a person under political and social oppression.

column2: To take precautions from the outset so as not to end up blaming anyone.
column3: To tie one's donkey to a sturdy stake.
column4: The full form of the proverb is eşeğini sağlam kazığa bağla, komşunu hırsız çıkarma 'tie your donkey to a sturdy stake and do not make a thief of your neighbor'. In the village, animals are tied to a stake in the yard at night; when a donkey that slips free of a loose stake goes missing, suspicion falls on the neighbor. The saying advises taking one's own precautions before blaming others and reflects a concern to protect neighborly relations.

column2: Whoever breaks away from the community is left exposed to danger.
column3: The wolf snatches the sheep that strays from the flock.
column4: In shepherd culture the flock is a whole under the protection of the shepherd and his dogs; a lone sheep wandering to the edge of the pasture is the wolf's first target. The Yörük and Türkmen communities who practiced seasonal transhumance taught this truth to children from an early age. The proverb has become a rule of life counseling the individual's loyalty to the community.

column2: Upbringing and discipline must be given at an early age.
column3: A tree is bent while it is still a sapling.
column4: In gardening and viticulture a sapling is tied to a stake and trained in the first years after planting; once the trunk has turned woody it can no longer be shaped and breaks if forced. This observation was transferred to the upbringing of children. The saying appears in books of counsel and proverb collections from the 16th century onward.

column2: To go after something almost impossible to find.
column3: To look for a needle in the hayloft.
column4: The samanlık is the enclosed space where dry straw stored as winter fodder is piled; a small object dropped into it disappears among the heap. A needle, being thin and close to the color of straw, is the hardest object of all to find. The idiom arose from this village reality and gave Turkish its version of a common comparison that exists with the same image in many languages.

column2: To confuse things that are quite different, failing to tell them apart.
column3: To mix up the stalks with the chaff.
column4: After the threshing sledge has been driven over the grain, the crop is separated into three products: kernel, fine chaff (saman) and coarse stalk (sap). Chaff is animal fodder, while stalks serve as fuel and building material; separating the two is one of the basic tasks of threshing. Through the image of a clumsy villager unable to make this distinction, the idiom describes a person who confuses concepts.

column2: A destructive element smuggled into the enemy's midst; a disguised threat.
column3: The wooden horse brought into the city of Troy.
column4: According to the legend told in Homer's Odyssey and Virgil's Aeneid, the Achaeans captured Troy, which they had besieged for ten years, by means of a wooden horse in which they hid soldiers. The ruins of Troy were excavated at Hisarlık, Çanakkale, in the 1870s. The expression entered Turkish from Western languages at the end of the 19th century and has been carried into the present through its use for computer viruses.

column2: A problem that cannot be solved by ordinary means but can be overcome by one decisive stroke.
column3: The knot in the city of Gordion.
column4: Gordion, near Polatlı, was the capital of Phrygia. According to ancient authors, it was believed that whoever untied the knot binding King Gordias's wagon to the temple would rule Asia; in 333 BC Alexander the Great, instead of untying the knot, cut it with his sword. Arrian and Plutarch relate the episode. The expression, echoed in Turkish by the idiom kesip atmak 'to cut it off', became established in the press of the Republican period.

column2: The weakest, most vulnerable point of a powerful person or structure.
column3: The heel of Achilles.
column4: According to legend, when his mother Thetis dipped Achilles into the river Styx to make him immortal she held him by the heel, so only his heel remained vulnerable. This detail is absent from Homer; the story took shape in the Achilleid of the Roman poet Statius (1st century). The expression also lives on in Western medical language as the Achilles tendon, and it entered Turkish in the Republican period.

column2: A dangerous subject that, once opened, leads to one evil after another.
column3: Pandora's box.
column4: In Hesiod's Works and Days, Pandora, the first woman created by Zeus, opens a vessel containing all the world's troubles; only hope remains at the bottom. In the ancient text the vessel is a pithos, a large storage jar; the sense 'box' became established in the 16th century through a word choice in Erasmus's Latin translation. Turkish took the expression in this Western form.

column2: A danger that may strike at any moment and keeps one in constant unease.
column3: The sword hanging over the head of Damocles.
column4: As Cicero relates in his Tusculanae Disputationes, Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, seated his flatterer Damocles, who envied his reign, on the throne and had a sword hung above his head by a single horsehair. The story conveys that power is full of unseen threats. The expression entered Turkish via French and has been used frequently in political writing.

column2: A victory that costs the winner so dearly that it amounts to a defeat.
column3: The victory of King Pyrrhus.
column4: Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, defeated the Roman armies at Heraclea and Asculum in 280 and 279 BC but lost his best soldiers. According to Plutarch, the king said that one more such victory would utterly ruin him. The expression passed from Western historiography into Turkish through military and political commentary.

column2: The most brilliant and happiest period of a society, an art or a person.
column3: An age made of gold.
column4: Hesiod named the ages of humankind after metals and counted the first age, when Cronus reigned and people lived free of care and in abundance, as the golden age. Ovid uses the same sequence in the Metamorphoses. In Turkish the expression is used for every field, such as the Ottoman Empire's period of ascendancy or an artist's most productive years.

column2: To make an offer of peace and reconciliation.
column3: To hand someone an olive branch.
column4: In ancient Greece the olive was regarded as Athena's gift to Athens; suppliants and envoys of peace carried olive branches in their hands. In the Hebrew Bible, Noah's dove likewise announces the end of the flood with an olive leaf. The olive branch, a shared symbol of the Mediterranean, entered Turkish as an idiom from the language of international diplomacy.

column2: Everyone must be given the share, authority or credit they deserve.
column3: Render unto Caesar what is Caesar's.
column4: The saying occurs in the Gospel of Matthew 22:21: asked about taxes, Jesus points to a coin bearing the emperor's image and says that what is Caesar's should be given to Caesar and what is God's to God. In Western languages the formula is used for the separation of worldly and religious authority; in Turkish it is said mostly in the sense of giving someone their due.

column2: To take a resolute step from which there is no turning back.
column3: To cross the river Rubicon.
column4: The Rubicon was the boundary river in northern Italy between the province of Rome and Gaul; for a commander to cross it with his army counted as rebellion against the Senate. According to Suetonius, Caesar said 'the die is cast' as he crossed the river in 49 BC. The idiom entered Turkish from European languages through the language of political commentary.

column2: Different paths and methods ultimately lead to the same goal.
column3: Every road reaches Rome.
column4: The Roman Empire built its paved roads running from the capital to the provinces as a single network; the golden milestone erected in the Forum was regarded as the starting point of all roads. This saying, uttered in Latin in the Middle Ages, also bears traces of the Roman roads in Anatolia. It passed into Turkish by translation from Western languages.

column2: A complex, insidious intrigue; a devious trick.
column3: A game typical of Byzantium.
column4: The Byzantine court is known for its struggles over the throne, disgracings and punishments by blinding; this is why the adjective 'byzantine' took on the meaning of convoluted intrigue in Western languages. In Turkish the expression has been used in political writing from the late 19th century onward, especially to describe Istanbul-centered power struggles, and it also reflects the Ottoman view of its former neighbor.

column2: Idealized love without sexual desire, often left unrequited.
column3: Love in the manner of Plato.
column4: In Plato's dialogue the Symposium, love is defined as a path ascending from bodily beauty to spiritual beauty and finally to the good itself. The Renaissance thinker Marsilio Ficino referred to this conception as amor platonicus, and the term spread into Western languages from there. In Turkish the meaning has narrowed, and it is used for unrequited love or love from afar.

column2: Do not help me; it is enough that you do not stand in my way.
column3: Do not cast your shadow on me; I ask no other favor.
column4: According to an anecdote related by Plutarch, Alexander the Great asked the philosopher Diogenes, who was sunbathing in Corinth, what he wished for; Diogenes asked him to step out of his sun. The story entered Ottoman books of ethics as well and took this pithy formulaic shape in Turkish. It sums up the Cynic philosophy's attitude of contentment with little.

column2: Hard to find one's way out of; winding and complex.
column3: Like a labyrinth.
column4: According to the ancient account, King Minos of Crete had his master craftsman Daedalus build a structure with no findable exit in order to imprison the Minotaur; Theseus escaped from it thanks to Ariadne's thread. The complex plan of the palace of Knossos may have given rise to the legend. The word entered Turkish via French labyrinthe and is used as a metaphor for bazaars and bureaucracy.

column2: To be on the verge of happening.
column3: To be standing with one's hand on one's ear.
column4: The muezzin raises his hand to his ear as he begins to recite the call to prayer; this gesture both strengthens the voice and signals that the call is about to begin. Anyone who saw the muezzin on the minaret with his hand on his ear knew that the time for prayer had come. Starting from this image, the idiom came to be used for anything that is about to happen at any moment.

column2: For an envious or admiring gaze to cause harm to someone.
column3: For a gaze to touch.
column4: The Arabic word nazar means 'gaze'; the belief that the evil eye causes harm is documented in Mesopotamia and Anatolia since antiquity, and the Qur'an's Surah al-Falaq contains a plea for refuge from the evil of the envier. Practices such as the blue bead, burning harmal seeds and pouring molten lead are connected to this belief. The verb değmek 'to touch' in the idiom shows that the gaze was conceived as a physical contact.

column2: A phrase said in the hope that a situation going well will not be spoiled.
column3: May lead be poured into the devil's ear.
column4: According to folk belief, the devil tries to spoil good news when he hears it; stopping his ear with lead means deafening him. The Anatolian practice of pouring molten lead against the evil eye and fright rests on the same idea. The formula is uttered immediately after good news is mentioned, as a kind of protective prayer.

column2: To feel overwhelming love and devotion for someone; to give everything for someone's sake.
column3: To be offered as a sacrifice.
column4: Arabic qurbān denotes the animal slaughtered in order to draw near to God, and its root is the same as that of qarīb 'near'. Abraham's readiness to sacrifice his son is recounted in the Qur'an as the symbol of submission. In Turkish the idiom, with the sense of being ready to give one's life for a loved one, has become a term of endearment in popular speech.

column2: A phrase said in the face of an unexpected situation that human reason cannot explain.
column3: God's doing.
column4: In folk belief every event is the work of divine will; developments such as inexplicable coincidences or miracles are met with this phrase. Similar formulas are frequent in Ottoman-era hagiographies and travel accounts. The saying expresses both astonishment and acceptance, and is sometimes used together with takdir-i ilahi 'divine decree'.

column2: Very old; outdated.
column3: Left over from the time of the Prophet Noah.
column4: Noah is mentioned in the Qur'an and the Hebrew Bible as the prophet who lived before the flood and reached the age of nine hundred and fifty; in folk narrative he is the symbol of the most ancient time. In Ottoman Turkish the word nebi was used in the sense of 'prophet'. The idiom hyperbolically describes an object or an idea as old enough to belong to the time before the flood.

column2: To come to someone's aid at exactly the right moment, when least expected.
column3: To arrive to the rescue like Hızır.
column4: Hızır (al-Khidr) is the figure identified with the unnamed wise man in the Qur'an's Surah al-Kahf, held to be immortal and believed to help those in distress. In Anatolia the Hıdrellez festivities celebrate his meeting with Ilyas (Elijah). The idiom is the most widespread reflection of this folk belief; Hızır is believed to appear on a grey horse or in the guise of a white-bearded old man.

column1: kırk yıllık Kâni olur mu Yani
column2: Deep-rooted habits and identity do not change easily.
column3: Can a Kâni of forty years become a Yani?
column4: Yani is a name common among the Greeks (Rum), while Kâni is a Muslim name. The full form of the saying conveys that someone who takes the name Kâni cannot give up his old habits. The attitude behind the saying is the caution with which converts were regarded in Ottoman society. Today it has shed its religious meaning and is said only of the immutability of character.

column1: kısmetinde ne varsa kaşığında o çıkar
column2: A person obtains only what is destined for them.
column3: Whatever is in your lot comes up in your spoon.
column4: Arabic kısmet means 'share, apportionment'; in folk belief one's sustenance (rızk) is thought to be apportioned by God. At the Ottoman table, where food was eaten from a shared dish, the morsel that landed in each person's spoon symbolized their share. The proverb unites this table image with belief in fate and is said as a consolation that calms ambition.

column2: To recover from a grave illness or escape mortal danger.
column3: To tear through the shroud and come out.
column4: The kefen is the white cloth in which the dead are wrapped; in the past it was usual to prepare a shroud for a terminally ill person. The patient's recovery was imagined as the prepared shroud being torn up and going to waste. The idiom is used in popular speech in the sense of returning from the dead and rests on the identification of the shroud with death.

column2: To be certain of one's honesty and of being in the right; to have a clear conscience.
column3: To have no doubt about whether one's ritual ablution has been invalidated.
column4: In Islam, ritual ablution (abdest) is a prerequisite for prayer, and whoever doubts that it has been invalidated must renew it. A person sure of his ablution stands to prayer without fear. The idiom carried this rule of worship into the moral domain and came to describe the fearlessness of someone who knows he is innocent. A person who 'has doubts about his ablution', by contrast, is someone who feels guilty.

column2: To recoil from a remark or thought and ask forgiveness; absolutely not.
column3: I repent, I ask God's forgiveness.
column4: Arabic tevbe means 'to turn back from sin', and estağfirullah 'I ask God's forgiveness'. The plea for forgiveness (istiğfar), frequent in the Qur'an, became established in everyday speech as an exclamation. In Turkish the formula expresses the alarm of someone unwilling to utter a bad possibility, or modesty in the face of praise.

column2: A small portion set aside from food being eaten for onlookers, so that the evil eye does not strike.
column3: The eye's due.
column4: According to folk belief, failing to let someone who looks longingly at food taste it invites the evil eye, so a piece is given to the onlooker. The notion of göz hakkı is the union of the evil-eye belief with the custom of sharing at the table. Today the idiom carries all three senses: giving a share, protecting against the evil eye and giving someone their due.

column2: To be believed to bring blessing and good fortune to the place one arrives at.
column3: To arrive with a lucky foot.
column4: In Old Turkic, uğur means 'road' and 'time'; from this the sense of good fortune developed. In Anatolia, if good things happen after a bride, a baby or a guest enters a house, this is attributed to that person's foot. Someone whose foot is considered unlucky is approached with caution. The idiom is the reflection of folk belief in human relationships.

column2: A reckless person who recognizes no moral limit whatsoever.
column3: Fears not God, is not ashamed before man.
column4: In Islamic ethics, fear of God and shame before people are regarded as the two fundamental brakes that restrain behavior. The idiom, said of a person who recognizes neither limit, appears in books of counsel and in Ottoman popular speech. The word kul here means a human being, as God's creature.

column2: Stubborn; never backing down from what one has said.
column3: Says 'Noah' but will not say 'prophet'.
column4: According to the account, someone forced to change religion or questioning his faith refused to acknowledge Noah's prophethood, uttering his name but not his title. The story has no documented source; the idiom is also connected with the Qur'anic account of Noah failing to persuade his people for nine hundred years. Today it conveys stubbornness alone.

column2: For the forty-day period following a birth or a death to be completed.
column3: For the forty days to be completed.
column4: In Anatolian folk belief the forty days following birth, death and marriage are a transitional period in which a person is considered unprotected; the new mother and baby are not left alone during this time, and the period is closed with the ritual washing known as kırk suyu. The number forty is also held sacred through the Qur'anic account of Moses and the forty-day retreat of Sufi practice. The idiom describes this custom.

column2: To become tiresome through constant repetition.
column3: To leave a taste as bland as squash.
column4: Squash is a cheap and plentiful vegetable in Anatolian cuisine but has no distinctive flavor of its own; its appearance on the table every day all summer breeds weariness. The idiom describes a joke or remark repeated for a long time becoming as insipid and tedious as a squash dish. In Turkish, squash is the one vegetable identified with blandness.

column2: To live comfortably, with no worries about making a living.
column3: To have salt that has not gone damp.
column4: Salt was the only way to keep winter meat, cheese and pickles from spoiling; salt that absorbs moisture cakes and becomes useless. A household that could keep its salt dry had both a dry, sound larder and sufficient provisions. Starting from this larder reality, the idiom describes a carefree, well-off person, sometimes in a reproachful tone.

column1: sütten ağzı yanan yoğurdu üfleyerek yer
column2: Someone who has been hurt once behaves with excessive caution in similar situations.
column3: One whose mouth was burned by milk blows even on cold yogurt before eating it.
column4: Yogurt is made by boiling milk before it is cultured; someone who has scalded their tongue on hot milk cannot eat even yogurt they know to be cold without blowing on it. Yogurt is the food the early Turks contributed to world cuisine, and its name appears in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk. Through this kitchen scene the proverb mocks the excessive caution born of experience.

column2: To spoil a nearly finished piece of work at the last moment.
column3: To add water to cooked food.
column4: Aş means 'food' in Old Turkic and is used especially for pilaf and soup. If water is added to cooked pilaf, the grains fall apart and the flavor is lost, which is why cooks measure the water from the start. The idiom describes the damage done by someone who interferes needlessly in a completed task through this kitchen error.

column2: To flatter and fawn for personal gain.
column3: To lick the food bowl.
column4: The çanak is a wide food bowl made of earthenware or copper; the person who licks the bottom of the bowl after a meal is someone content with his master's leftovers. The fact that the household retainers of Ottoman mansions lived on leftovers from the table gave rise to this comparison. The expression çanak yalayıcı, from the same root, is used in the sense of 'toady'.

column2: To make a bad situation even worse; to embellish an account provocatively.
column3: To sprinkle salt and pepper on top.
column4: Salt and pepper are the final touches that sharpen the taste of a dish, while rubbing salt into a wound increases pain. The idiom combines both senses: someone who 'adds salt and pepper' to a story makes it more bitter and more inflammatory. The arrival of red pepper in Anatolia from the Americas in the 16th century suggests that the idiom is no older than the Ottoman period.

column1: bir fincan kahvenin kırk yıl hatırı vardır
column2: Even a small act of hospitality creates a lasting bond of gratitude.
column3: A cup of coffee is remembered for forty years.
column4: Coffee came to Istanbul from Yemen in the 16th century, and the first coffeehouses opened around 1554; Kâtip Çelebi recounts the controversies coffee caused in his Mizânü'l-Hak. For a time coffee was an expensive drink whose offering was a valued gesture. The proverb is the product of coffee's transformation into a symbol of conversation and friendship; the number forty here expresses abundance.

column2: Two people alike in character have found each other.
column3: The pot rolled and found its lid.
column4: Copper pots and their lids are made as matching sets; not every lid fits every pot. A rolling pot coming to rest right beside its own lid describes the meeting of two things that match each other. The proverb is usually mocking, said of two ill-natured people who have found one another. A similar saying exists in European languages.

column2: To devalue a kindness one has done by the bad behavior that follows it.
column3: To give food with a spoon and then poke out an eye with its handle.
column4: At the Ottoman table food was eaten from a shared dish with wooden spoons, and for elders to give a morsel to the young was considered an act of generosity. Jabbing the handle of the same spoon into someone's eye is the exact opposite of that generosity. Through this table image the idiom conveys the hurt caused when kindness and cruelty come from the same hand.

column2: To live off others without working at all.
column3: Bread from another's hand, water from the lake.
column4: The idiom describes a person who has no field or well of his own and gets his bread from a neighbor's hand and his water from the common lake. In Anatolia bread was produced by the household's own labor, while water usually came from the village's shared source. Someone who contributed labor to neither was reproached; the idiom is a softened, sometimes envious, form of that reproach.

column2: An oath-like phrase said of anyone who goes back on their word or resolve.
column3: May the spoon of whoever turns away from the pilaf be broken.
column4: Pilaf was the most prized dish of the Ottoman and Anatolian table; it came at the end of wedding and holiday feasts and was eaten with spoons from a shared tray. A broken wooden spoon means going without food. The formula reinforces the promise that people embarking on a venture make to one another with this custom of the pilaf table.

column2: Whoever handles something valuable takes a share of it for himself.
column3: Whoever holds the honey jar licks his finger.
column4: Before sugar became widespread, honey was the only sweetener and was stored in jars; it is natural for the person ladling out honey to lick what sticks to his finger. The proverb likens this small taste to those who manage public property setting aside a share for themselves. It is said in a tone both of tolerance and of criticism.

column2: To appreciate good food and good things; to have taste.
column3: To know the taste of one's own mouth.
column4: Ottoman cuisine reached hundreds of dishes in the hands of palace and mansion cooks, and a refined palate was regarded as a measure of sophistication. The idiom praises a person able to discriminate flavors; in time it came to be used for preferences beyond food as well. The idiom ağzının tadı kaçmak, by contrast, describes the disturbance of one's peace of mind.

column2: To take the most profitable, most valuable part of a venture.
column3: To eat the cream of the milk.
column4: The kaymak that collects on top of milk after it is boiled and left to stand is the milk's richest and most valuable part; once it is taken, only thin milk remains. Water-buffalo kaymak was an especially favored treat in Ottoman Istanbul. The idiom describes someone who grabs the best part of a venture through the image of leaving the thin milk to the others.

column2: To have made a contribution, however small, to getting something done.
column3: To have one's own salt in the soup.
column4: Everyone contributed an ingredient to the communal soup cooked in a shared cauldron during collective work (imece); salt is the smallest and cheapest of these, yet there is no soup without salt. The idiom takes its sense of a small but necessary contribution from this communal table. It is a modest way of speaking: someone who says çorbada tuzum olsun wants not a large share but simply to have contributed.

column2: To put someone off with a small promise; to placate.
column3: To smear a fingerful of honey in someone's mouth.
column4: Smearing honey in a newborn's mouth to stop its crying was a widespread practice in Anatolia; the tradition of tahnik, performed with dates, is similar. Honey does not satisfy hunger but keeps the child quiet for a while. Starting from this practice, the idiom describes a person deceived with a passing sweetness.

column2: To serve someone's interests unknowingly or unintentionally.
column3: To spread butter on someone's bread.
column4: Buttered bread was considered a luxury compared with plain bread; to butter someone's bread is to give them an unexpected benefit. The idiom is usually used in a negative context: whoever butters his adversary's bread has handed him an advantage with his own hands. Because ekmek 'bread' carries the sense of livelihood and earnings in Turkish, the comparison took root easily.

column2: To gather one's belongings in order to leave a place for good.
column3: To gather up one's bath bowl and comb.
column4: In Ottoman bathhouse culture women took their own bowl, comb, bath-wrap and clogs to the hamam in a bundle; gathering these up when leaving the bath was the sign of departure. The bowl and the comb are a person's two most personal belongings. From this scene of leaving the bathhouse, the idiom broadened to mean moving away from a place entirely.

column2: To adjust one's spending to one's income.
column3: To stretch one's feet only as far as the quilt reaches.
column4: The yorgan is a hand-sewn bedcover stuffed with cotton or wool; whoever stretches out too far under a short quilt gets cold. Yorgan is a word of Turkish origin and appears in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk. The idiom turned this plain domestic fact into a lesson in thrift; similar sayings exist in Arabic and Persian.

column2: To be overjoyed; to be unable to keep still for joy.
column3: For bells to ring on one's skirts.
column4: In Ottoman entertainment life, small bells were sewn onto the skirts or ankles of the çengi and köçek dancers and jingled as they danced. The skirts of someone bustling about with joy also ring out like these bells. Another account links the idiom to bells attached to bearers of good news, but this is not documented.

column2: Whoever undertakes a task must also bear its hardships.
column3: Whoever enters the bathhouse sweats.
column4: Someone who lies on the heated marble platform of an Ottoman hamam sweats in the heat and steam; it is impossible to enter a bathhouse and come out without sweating. The hamam passed from the Roman and Byzantine tradition to the Ottomans and was an institution found in every neighborhood. The proverb conveys accepting the natural consequences of a task from the outset through this bathhouse fact.

column2: To realize that the undertaking is dangerous and its cost high.
column3: The shoes are expensive.
column4: Pabuç comes from Persian pâpûş and denotes a leather shoe in the Ottoman period. Shoes being expensive means realizing that the affair will not come cheap; according to one account, whoever sees the danger flees even at the cost of losing his shoes. The idiom is generally used in the form pabucun pahalı olduğunu anlamak 'to realize the shoes are expensive'.

column2: To indulge in youthful excesses at an advanced age.
column3: To run wild after the age of forty.
column4: In popular understanding forty is the threshold at which a person matures and is expected to be dignified; the fact that prophethood came to Muhammad at forty reinforced this notion. The proverb kırkından sonra azanı teneşir paklar 'whoever runs wild after forty is cleansed only on the washing slab' is the idiom's full form. The saying harshly condemns behavior unbecoming to one's age.

column2: Generous; unsparing with money and help.
column3: Open-handed.
column4: A closed fist symbolizes stinginess and an open palm giving; in Anatolia, where hospitality is a high value, open-handedness is praise. The Kutadgu Bilig counts generosity among the fundamental virtues of a ruler (bey). The idiom is a universal comparison born of a hand gesture, and its opposite eli sıkı 'tight-handed' uses the same image.

column2: The people around a dwelling matter more than the dwelling itself.
column3: Do not buy a house, buy a neighbor.
column4: The Ottoman neighborhood (mahalle) was a community in which the imam and the residents stood surety for one another; neighbors relied on each other in sickness, at funerals and at weddings. A bad neighbor could be grounds for expulsion from the neighborhood in court records. The proverb makes this solidarity the first criterion in choosing a house.

column2: A guest must be content with what the host can provide.
column3: The guest eats not what he hoped for but what he finds.
column4: In Anatolia a guest is honored by the household offering its best food, but for the guest to expect more than this is considered rude. The proverb recalls the guest's side of this rule of mutual courtesy. The word misafir comes from Arabic müsâfir 'traveler'.

column2: Immediately upon arriving from a journey, without resting at all.
column3: With the dust of the road still on one's feet.
column4: In the era of travel on dirt roads, a traveler arriving home had shoes and trousers covered in dust, and was expected first to wash and rest. Someone who gets to work 'with the dust on his feet' has skipped this rest. The idiom is an everyday trace of Ottoman caravan and post-station travel.

column1: bir eli yağda bir eli balda
column2: To live in plenty and prosperity.
column3: One hand dipped in butter, the other in honey.
column4: Butter and honey are the two most valued foods of the Anatolian table; a household possessing both at once was considered wealthy. At the end of folktales it is said that the bride and groom lived with one hand in butter and the other in honey. The idiom passed from this folktale formula into everyday speech and has become the best-known expression of prosperity.

column2: A shameless person who never gives up, no matter what.
column3: Chased out the door, he comes in through the chimney.
column4: In old Anatolian houses the hearth chimney was wide and opened onto the roof; children and thieves could enter the house through it. Someone driven out by the door who returns through the chimney is a shameless person who refuses to accept being turned away. The idiom arose from this feature of domestic architecture and in time came to be used for the persistent person.

column2: People usually fail to see the problems of those closest to them.
column3: A candle does not light its own base.
column4: In homes before electricity, candles and oil lamps were the only source of light; the flame casts light upward and sideways, while the base of the candle remains in shadow. This observation turned into a lesson describing the scholar or wealthy person who cannot benefit his own household. The saying is found in similar form in Persian and Arabic.

column2: I do not believe what you are saying.
column3: Tell that to my cap.
column4: The külah is the pointed felt cap of the Ottoman period, worn by many groups such as janissaries and dervishes. The idiom presents the cap on the listener's head as if it were the audience, conveying that the words are not taken seriously; being lifeless, the cap believes everything. Someone who offers his cap rather than his head does not consider the words worth even listening to.

column2: To be bedridden for a long time with a serious illness.
column3: To lie in quilt and mattress.
column4: In the traditional house the mattress (döşek) was put away in the bedding cupboard by day and laid out only at night; someone who stays in quilt and mattress during the day is seriously ill. The idiom arose from this rule of household order. Yorgan and döşek are two words of Turkish origin recorded in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk.

column2: To expose someone's hidden faults and disgraces.
column3: To dump the dirty laundry out in front of everyone.
column4: Laundry was once washed collectively at the fountain or in the bathhouse, and for dirty laundry to be seen was considered shameful. Through the image of dumping the household's hidden filth into the street, the idiom describes the exposure of private life. The same comparison exists in French, and it may also have been reinforced in Turkish through translation in the 19th century.

column2: To be extremely arrogant; to tolerate not even the slightest criticism.
column3: To allow no hair to be plucked from one's nose.
column4: Plucking a nose hair is both painful and a humiliating intrusion; someone who does not allow it rejects every kind of touch. The nose is the organ of pride in Turkish: idioms such as burnu büyümek 'to have a swollen nose' and burnu havada 'nose in the air' belong to the same family. The idiom conveys the arrogant person's claim to untouchability through this bodily image.

column2: A worthless, base character.
column3: His liver is not worth even five para.
column4: At the butcher's, liver was considered so worthless, as the cheapest part of the meat, that it was thrown to the cats; five para was the smallest unit of coin. In folk medicine the liver was also regarded as the seat of courage and emotion, which is the source of the idiom ciğeri yanmak 'to have one's liver burn'. The idiom says that even a person's inner being is worth no more than the cheapest offal.

column2: To become exhausted; to emerge worn out from a hard task.
column3: To be left covered in blood and sweat.
column4: In heavy labor or in a fight the body sheds both sweat and blood from wounds; naming the two together marks the extreme point of exertion. The idiom comes from the language of tasks that depend on bodily strength, such as battle and threshing. Kan 'blood' and ter 'sweat' are two basic words in use since Old Turkic and entered this doublet easily.

column2: Very quiet, meek, not standing up for oneself.
column3: Has a mouth but no tongue.
column4: In Turkish dil is both the organ and the faculty of speech; a dilsiz person is one who cannot speak. The idiom describes a meek person who has a mouth yet does not use his tongue; it is said sometimes in praise and sometimes in pity. Idioms such as dili olmak 'to have a tongue' and dili uzun olmak 'to have a long tongue' are built on the same organ.

column2: To become arrogant, conceited.
column3: For one's nose to grow.
column4: Because the nose is the most prominent feature of the face, it has become identified with pride and a sense of superiority; the arrogant person raises his head and points his nose at the sky. Someone whose nose has grown sees himself as greater than he is. The idiom belongs to the same family of images as burnu havada 'nose in the air' and burnundan kıl aldırmamak 'to allow no hair plucked from one's nose'.

column2: To feel deep regret over a mistake one has made.
column3: To beat one's head against one stone after another.
column4: Beating the head in moments of mourning and regret was part of the lament tradition in Anatolia; at funerals women tore their hair and struck their heads against the wall. The idiom uses this gesture of mourning to convey the intensity of regret. A similar expression appears in the mourning scenes of the Dede Korkut narratives.

column2: Fearless of any danger; daring.
column3: Black-eyed.
column4: In Old Turkic kara denotes not only the color black but also strength and greatness; a 'black eye' is one that does not widen in fear but holds a steady gaze. The eye of a frightened person, by contrast, darts away and dims. The idiom conveys courage through the steadiness of the gaze and belongs to the same field as gözü pek 'firm-eyed' and gözünü budaktan sakınmamak 'not to shield one's eye from the branch'.

column2: To be so flustered as not to know what to do.
column3: For one's hands to get tangled in one's feet.
column4: The movements of an agitated person become confused, and the hands and feet lose their coordination; this picture is the source of the idiom. Folk medicine explained agitation as blood rushing to the head and believed it disrupted the coordination of the limbs. The idiom transferred this bodily observation to an emotional state.

column2: To endure hardship with patience.
column3: To press one's teeth together.
column4: A person enduring pain involuntarily clenches the teeth; in folk medicine, when a fracture or dislocation was being set, the patient was given a cloth to bite and told to clench the teeth. The idiom made this bodily reaction a symbol of patience. Clenching the teeth is also found in the descriptions of anger and endurance in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk.

column2: To feel an instant affinity for someone; to be lively and exuberant.
column3: For one's blood to boil.
column4: In the old medicine, human temperament was explained by the four humors; blood was considered hot and moist and the source of youth and cheerfulness. A person whose blood 'boils' grows exuberant under the influence of this warm temperament and forms bonds quickly. The idiom is one of the remnants of humoral theory in popular speech.

column2: To feel nauseous; to be disgusted by something.
column3: For one's bile to rise.
column4: Arabic safrâ means 'yellow' and in the old medicine denotes yellow bile, one of the four humors; its excess was held to cause nausea and anger. The bitter taste that rises to the mouth in nausea reinforced this idea. The idiom is a reflection in Ottoman folk medicine of the humoral theory inherited from the tradition of Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna).

column2: To be suddenly very frightened.
column3: For one's heart to rise up to one's mouth.
column4: In sudden fright the heart beats fast and feels as if it were pounding in the throat; in Old Turkic the word yürek denotes both the heart and courage. The idiom renders this bodily sensation in a plain image. Idioms such as yüreği yerinden oynamak 'for one's heart to leap from its place' and yüreği hop etmek 'for one's heart to jump' rest on the same observation.

column2: To become unable to speak from thirst or fear.
column3: For one's tongue to stick to one's palate.
column4: A person deprived of water produces less saliva and the tongue sticks to the palate; the same thing happens in intense fear. The idiom uses this physical symptom for both literal thirst and the inability to speak. The image of the tongue cleaving to the palate on the Day of Judgment occurs in Yunus Emre and in religious texts.

column2: Entirely, to the very depths.
column3: Right down to the bone marrow.
column4: Marrow (ilik) is the deepest tissue inside the bone; cold penetrating to the marrow means reaching the innermost layer of the body. In folk medicine marrow was regarded as the source of strength, and marrow broth was drunk as a cure. The idiom is used to express depth and completeness in forms such as iliklerine kadar ıslanmak 'to be soaked to the marrow' and iliklerine kadar hissetmek 'to feel to the marrow'.

column2: To surrender oneself to another's control; to give up one's will.
column3: To put one's beard into someone else's hand.
column4: In Ottoman society the beard was the symbol of a man's dignity; laying a hand on a man's beard was a grave insult, and some punishments involved cutting off the beard. A man who puts his beard into someone's hand is considered to have surrendered his honor and his will. The idiom arose from this social meaning of the beard.

column2: To handle someone by behaving in accordance with their temperament and wishes.
column3: To give medicinal syrup according to the pulse.
column4: The old medicine regarded the pulse as the foundation of examination; by the speed and firmness of the pulse the physician prepared the şerbet, medicines in syrup form, for the patient. The idiom transferred this practice to the art of treating each person according to their nature. Şerbet comes from the Arabic root 'to drink' and in the Ottoman period meant both a beverage and a medicine.

column2: To be very young and inexperienced.
column3: For one's mouth to smell of milk.
column4: A nursing baby's breath smells of milk; this smell is the mark of a child not yet weaned. The idiom belittles an immature person by likening them to this sign of infancy. A similar expression exists in Arabic and Persian; the Turkish form comes from Ottoman popular speech.

column2: Corruption in a community begins with its leaders.
column3: A fish starts to stink from the head.
column4: Fresh fish begins to spoil first at the gills and internal organs in the head region; the fishmonger judges freshness by looking at the gills. This observation turned into a political lesson that decay begins at the top. The saying also exists in Mediterranean languages such as Greek and Italian; the fish-market culture of Ottoman Istanbul supported the Turkish form.

column2: To appear resilient and cheerful even in hard times.
column3: To hold one's tail up straight.
column4: Cats and dogs carry their tails erect when healthy and confident; a sick or frightened animal tucks its tail between its legs. The idiom transferred this animal behavior to human bearing. The daily observation of cats in Ottoman street-animal culture helped the idiom spread.

column2: To commit massive embezzlement; to pocket everything at once.
column3: To swallow the camel together with its pack-saddle.
column4: The hamut is the padded collar of felt and leather placed around the neck of a camel or horse for fastening loads; to swallow the camel with its hamut is to take not only the goods but their container too. The idiom was used in the 19th-century Ottoman press to describe the corruption of officials. Because the camel was the most valuable pack animal in caravan trade, it became a measure of magnitude.

column1: kedi gibi dört ayak üstüne düşmek
column2: To escape every danger unharmed.
column3: To land on all four feet like a cat.
column4: A cat falling from a height turns in the air and lands on its four feet; this ability is one of the reasons for the folk belief that a cat has nine lives. Born of this observation, the idiom describes a lucky and resourceful person. Because the cat was cherished as a domestic animal in Ottoman Istanbul, it found a frequent place in everyday speech.

column2: To beat someone long and very hard.
column3: To beat someone until the donkey comes back from the water.
column4: In the village the donkey was taken to the fountain or stream in the morning to carry water, and its return took a long time; a beating lasting that long conveys the length of the beating. Some interpretations explain sudan gelmek as the donkey wandering off on its own and coming back. In any case the idiom uses the time scale of village life.

column2: Ill-intentioned people take advantage of times of confusion.
column3: The wolf loves misty, hazy weather.
column4: According to shepherds' observation, the wolf approaches the flock in fog and hazy weather, when the shepherd and dogs notice it late. The Dede Korkut narratives also stress the wolf's association with night and darkness. The proverb applies this observation to people who profit from turmoil; duman here means 'mist'.

column2: To be very weak and frail.
column3: To have as much life as a bird.
column4: Small birds like sparrows are almost weightless when held in the hand and die easily; the word can here means both life and body. The idiom likens the fragility of a small bird to a weak person. Kuş kadar canı olmak is usually said with tenderness, sometimes dismissively.

column2: To perform an extraordinary feat; no matter what one does.
column3: To catch a bird with one's mouth.
column4: Catching a flying bird with the mouth is an impossible feat; the idiom is usually used in a negative construction: ağzıyla kuş tutsa beğendiremez 'even if he caught a bird with his mouth he could not please them'. It survives from the era when bird hunting was widespread at court and among the people. The idiom conveys that even the greatest skill will not satisfy some people.

column2: To lose one's mind; to go mad.
column3: To let one's goats get away.
column4: The goat is an animal that climbs rocks, easily breaks from the herd and is hard to control; for a goatherd to lose his goats means losing his job and his reputation. The idiom's sense of losing one's mind rests on unruly and uncontrolled behavior like a goat's. The word keçi has become identified in Turkish with obstinacy and headstrongness.

column2: To exaggerate and blow up something trivial.
column3: To make a flea the size of a camel.
column4: The flea is the smallest animal and the camel the largest in Anatolia; the difference in size between the two became the measure of exaggeration. The idiom was formed in Ottoman popular speech with these two extremes. The camel serves as a measure of magnitude in many Turkish idioms, such as deve kadar 'as big as a camel' and deveyi hamuduyla yutmak 'to swallow the camel with its pack-saddle'.

column1: tavşan dağa küsmüş dağın haberi olmamış
column2: The resentment of the weak has no effect whatsoever on the powerful.
column3: The hare took offense at the mountain, and the mountain never knew.
column4: The hare is among the most timid and insignificant animals living on the mountain, while the mountain does not even notice it. The proverb conveys the pointlessness of a small person's resentment toward a great one through this image from nature. In Anatolia the mountain is a symbol both of refuge and of unshakable power; the hare's sulking changes nothing for the mountain.

column2: Worthless criticism cannot stop great undertakings from going forward.
column3: The dog barks, the caravan moves on.
column4: As caravans passed through villages the dogs barked, but the laden camels walked on unconcerned. This scene, an everyday sight on the Silk Road and the caravan routes of Anatolia, turned into a lesson in perseverance. The saying also exists in Persian and Arabic; it became established in Turkish together with caravan culture.

column2: People belittle what they cannot obtain.
column3: The cat calls the liver it cannot reach unclean.
column4: Liver hanging in the butcher's shop is the cats' favorite food; a cat that cannot reach it pretends not to care for it. Mundar comes from Persian murdar and denotes something considered religiously unclean. The proverb conveys the same idea as Aesop's fable of the fox and the grapes through a scene of an Ottoman street cat and a butcher.

column1: horozu çok olan köyün sabahı geç olur
column2: Where there are too many people in charge, work does not progress.
column3: In a village with many roosters, morning comes late.
column4: The rooster is the animal that announces morning in the village; when roosters multiply, each crows at a different hour and the villagers do not know which to trust. With this humorous observation the proverb conveys the harm of having too many heads. The Kutadgu Bilig too says that two rulers in one country will upset its order; the same idea lives on in popular speech through the image of the rooster.

column2: It is too late; there is nothing more to be done.
column3: Whoever took the horse has already passed Üsküdar.
column4: Üsküdar was the starting point of the road from Istanbul into Anatolia; a horse thief who had crossed the Bosphorus was considered to have escaped his pursuers. According to tradition, the idiom goes back to Köroğlu, who stole the horse of the Bey of Bolu, or to an Istanbul thief, but these stories are not documented. In any case the idiom survives from an era when horse theft was common.

column1: koyun can derdinde kasap et derdinde
column2: Everyone thinks of their own interest; the plight of the weak does not concern the powerful.
column3: The sheep thinks of saving its life, the butcher of getting meat.
column4: The slaughter of a sheep for sacrifice or for the butcher was an ordinary scene of village life; while the sheep struggles to escape, the butcher reckons only the meat. The proverb is born of the striking picture of these opposed interests. The sheep, as the Turks' oldest domestic animal, represents the weak side in many proverbs.

column2: To eliminate a danger before it grows.
column3: To crush the snake's head while it is small.
column4: In rural Anatolia the snake is the chief enemy of the house and the sheepfold; a young snake was killed early because it would be venomous when grown. Starting from this practice, the idiom advises solving small problems before they grow. The belief that a snake does not die unless its head is crushed explains the idiom's emphasis on the head.

column1: tilkinin dönüp dolaşıp geleceği yer kürkçü dükkânıdır
column2: However far one strays from an inevitable outcome, one arrives at it in the end.
column3: However much the fox roams, it ends up at the furrier's shop.
column4: Fox fur was among the most valuable furs in the Ottoman period, and the furriers' guild was concentrated around the Grand Bazaar. The pelt of the fox that flees the hunter ultimately reaches the furrier. The proverb conveys that cunning cannot change fate through this image of hunting and trade; the fox is the symbol of cunning in Turkish.

column2: To invent absurd excuses for a task one does not want to do.
column3: To spread flour on a rope.
column4: According to a Nasreddin Hoca anecdote, a neighbor asks to borrow his clothesline; the Hoca says they have spread flour on it. When the neighbor objects that flour cannot be spread on a rope, the Hoca replies that it can when one does not want to lend it. The anecdote appears in manuscripts from the 16th century onward, and the idiom has become the best-known expression for making excuses.

column2: Whoever pays the price gets what they want.
column3: Whoever pays the money plays the whistle.
column4: According to a Nasreddin Hoca anecdote, children ask the Hoca, who is going to market, for whistles; only one of them gives him money. On his return the Hoca gives the whistle to that child alone and says parayı veren düdüğü çalar. The anecdote conveys the futility of asking for something for nothing; the proverb is still frequently used in commerce and politics.

column2: The lesson to be drawn from a story.
column3: The share taken from the tale.
column4: Arabic kıssa means 'story' and hisse 'share'. In the tradition of the mesnevi and the book of counsel (nasihatname), every story ends with a section drawing the moral, and these sections bear the heading kıssadan hisse. The expression passed from Ottoman didactic literature into popular speech and is said today of the lesson to be drawn from an event.

column2: A saying that criticizes those who value people for their clothes rather than their character.
column3: Eat, my fur coat, eat.
column4: According to a Nasreddin Hoca anecdote, the Hoca is ignored at a feast he attends in his old clothes; when he returns wearing his fur coat he is seated in the place of honor. The Hoca dips his fur coat into the food and says ye kürküm ye. The anecdote is a critique of treatment based on appearance, and the formula recalls that critique in a single sentence.

column2: The acceptance of an unbelievable lie when self-interest is involved.
column3: For a cauldron to give birth.
column4: Nasreddin Hoca returns a cauldron borrowed from his neighbor with a small pot inside it and says the cauldron has given birth; the neighbor accepts gladly. The second time he borrows the cauldron he does not return it and says it has died. The anecdote describes the person who does not question what suits his interest, and the idiom lives on in this sense.

column2: A dispute ends once the real cause of the quarrel is removed.
column3: The quilt is gone, the fight is over.
column4: According to a Nasreddin Hoca anecdote, the Hoca, curious about a fight in the street at night, goes outside wrapped in his quilt; the brawlers snatch the quilt and run off. Returning home, the Hoca tells his wife that the fight was over the quilt. The anecdote humorously describes the nature of conflicts of interest, and the idiom was born from it.

column2: Above every powerful person there is someone more powerful.
column3: One hand is above another.
column4: The proverb's full form is el elden üstündür, arşa çıkınca kadar 'one hand is above another, all the way up to the heavenly throne'; arş is the highest level of the heavens. The saying appears in similar forms in the literature of counsel from the Kutadgu Bilig onward and is used at the end of folktales as a warning that humbles the hero's pride. It is a lesson in humility.

column2: To last very long and in great splendor (of weddings, festivities).
column3: For forty days and forty nights.
column4: In folktales and epics the hero's wedding lasts forty days and forty nights; feasts are described with this formula in the Dede Korkut narratives as well. The number forty expresses completeness and abundance in Turkish and Islamic culture: kırklar 'the Forty Saints', kırk hırsız 'forty thieves', kırkı çıkmak 'to complete the forty days'. The formula passed from the language of folktales into everyday hyperbole.

column2: The opening of a folktale; an introduction to a narrative whose truth is uncertain.
column3: Once there was, once there was not.
column4: This is the opening formula of the Turkish folktale and usually continues with the words evvel zaman içinde, kalbur saman içinde. The opposition of var 'there was' and yok 'there was not' announces from the start that what is told lies between reality and fantasy. The formula comes from the oral tradition of Anatolian storytellers and is also said jokingly today of dubious accounts.

column2: The closing formula of a folktale; the narrative ending happily.
column3: Three apples fell from the sky.
column4: Turkish folktales end with three apples falling from the sky: one for the teller, one for the listener and one for the hero of the tale. The apple is a symbol of abundance and fertility in Anatolian and Central Asian culture; within the tale, the apple given by a dervish enables a couple to have a child. The formula is found in similar form in Armenian and Kurdish folktales as well.

column1: dağ dağa kavuşmaz insan insana kavuşur
column2: However far apart people may fall, they may one day meet again.
column3: Mountain does not meet mountain, but person meets person.
column4: The reunion of separated lovers and siblings is a frequent motif in folk narratives; stories such as Kerem ile Aslı and Tahir ile Zühre carry this hope. The proverb voices that hope through the contrast between mountains, which are fixed, and people, who move. Similar words occur in the folk songs of exile (gurbet türküleri).

column2: To accomplish seemingly impossible feats for the sake of one's beloved.
column3: To bore through mountains like Ferhat.
column4: In the folk romance Ferhat ile Şirin, Ferhat bores through a mountain near Amasya to bring water to the city in order to win Şirin; the story passed into Anatolian folk narrative from Nizâmî's mesnevi Hüsrev ü Şîrîn. The Ferhat water channel is still shown in Amasya today. The idiom is the symbol of great labor undertaken for love.

column2: To lose oneself in the pain of love and withdraw from everything.
column3: To take to the deserts like Mecnun.
column4: In the story of Leylâ ile Mecnûn, of Arabic origin, Kays loses his mind for love of Leylâ and lives in the deserts among wild animals; the name Mecnun means 'possessed by djinn'. Fuzûlî's mesnevi of 1535 made the story the best-known love narrative in Turkish literature. The idiom passed from this mesnevi into popular speech.

column2: A gang of robbers or corrupt people who have banded together for gain.
column3: Forty thieves.
column4: The story of Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves from the Thousand and One Nights reached Europe in the 18th century through French translation and from there Ottoman readers. Harami comes from the Arabic root haram and means a highway robber. The expression is used in political writing in the sense of an interest group; the phrase açıl susam açıl 'open sesame' comes from the same tale.

column2: In a place too far away to be reached.
column3: Behind Mount Kaf.
column4: In Islamic cosmography Kaf is the legendary mountain encircling the world, beyond which djinn and the Anka bird (the phoenix) live; in folktales the hero travels to the land of the fairies behind Mount Kaf. In Divan poetry the Anka and Kaf are mentioned together. The idiom left this folktale geography and acquired the meaning of very distant and inaccessible.

column1: bir deli kuyuya taş atmış kırk akıllı çıkaramamış
column2: A thoughtless act keeps many sensible people busy.
column3: One madman threw a stone into the well, and forty wise men could not get it out.
column4: A large stone thrown into a village well causes the water to recede and is very hard to remove. The proverb conveys this village reality through a folktale formula, the opposition of one madman and forty wise men. The number forty is the folktale's measure of multitude. The saying is used for things that are easily destroyed and hard to repair.

column2: To achieve an extraordinary success.
column3: To write an epic.
column4: Destan comes from Persian dâstân and denotes a long verse narrative of heroism; the epics of Köroğlu and Battal Gazi were recited in Anatolia for centuries. The idiom arose from the notion of an event being great enough to be the subject of an epic. Today it is frequently used in the language of sports and the press.

column2: To tell unreal, unconvincing things.
column3: To tell a fairy tale.
column4: Masal comes from Arabic mesel; in the past, on winter nights, storytellers and meddah performers told tales to gatherings, and this telling was called okumak 'reading, reciting'. Since everyone knew that a tale was not true, a person saying unbelievable things came to be told masal okuma 'do not tell tales'. The idiom is a trace of the oral narrative tradition left in the language.

column2: To become the talk of everyone; to become famous.
column3: To become an epic on every tongue.
column4: Epics were passed on from tongue to tongue by minstrels (âşık) to the accompaniment of the saz; for an event to become the subject of an epic was the widest form of dissemination. The idiom describes the spread of a person's beauty or the magnitude of an event by this means. The form adı dillere destan olmak occurs in folk poetry and folk songs.

column2: Never to be defeated; to remain strong always.
column3: For one's back never to touch the ground.
column4: In oil wrestling, defeat is decided when both of the wrestler's shoulders touch the ground; a wrestler whose back has not touched the ground is undefeated. The Kırkpınar wrestling tournament has been held since the 14th century, and the language of wrestling has given Turkish many idioms. The idiom is used in politics and business to express invincibility.

column2: To silence or defeat someone in an argument.
column3: To put the king in checkmate.
column4: Chess passed from India through Iran to the Islamic world and the Turks; the word mat is of Persian origin and denotes the king being left helpless. In the Ottoman period chess was widespread as a game of the palace and the coffeehouse, and the formula şah mat entered popular speech by this route. The idiom passed from the game board to the language of debate and took on the meaning of leaving one's opponent unable to reply.

column2: The unseen, secretly conducted side of events.
column3: Behind the curtain.
column4: In the Karagöz shadow play, the puppeteer (hayalî) stands behind a white screen and manipulates the figures without showing them to the audience, who see only the shadows. The theater curtain likewise conceals the backstage. The expression passed from this arrangement of the shadow theater into politics; the phrase perde arkasındaki güçler 'the powers behind the curtain' became established in the 19th-century press.

column2: To dance and make merry; to celebrate a joy exuberantly.
column3: To dance by shaking one's belly.
column4: Belly dancing was a dance based on movements of the abdomen and hips performed by the çengi dancers in Ottoman entertainment life; at weddings and festivities ordinary people also danced it. The idiom broadened this type of dance to the general sense of having fun. Today it is also said of celebrating a success joyfully.

column2: To embark on a venture leaving the outcome to chance.
column3: To throw the dice.
column4: Dice are the basic implement of backgammon, the most widespread game in Ottoman coffeehouses, and the outcome of the dice depends on chance. The idiom describes ventures that rely on luck. Caesar's words 'the die is cast' as he crossed the Rubicon use the same image; the Turkish form, however, comes from the culture of backgammon.

column2: To be defeated in wrestling by having one's back pinned to the ground; to suffer decisive defeat in a contest.
column3: To be touched down.
column4: Tuş comes from French touche and denotes both shoulders touching the mat in mat wrestling. The term became established when modern wrestling entered Turkey at the beginning of the 20th century and was added to the vocabulary of victory from oil wrestling. Today the idiom is used for decisive defeat in debate and politics.

column2: To use the strongest means at one's disposal.
column3: To play one's trump card.
column4: In card games the koz is the suit that beats all other cards; a player wins the hand by playing the trump at the right moment. The word is of French origin, and playing cards became widespread in Ottoman coffeehouses from the 18th century onward. The idiom passed from the gaming table into the language of bargaining and politics; the form kozunu paylaşmak is also used.

column2: To direct an affair or people from behind the scenes.
column3: To hold the puppet strings in one's hand.
column4: The string puppet show was an Ottoman entertainment in which the puppeteer moved the figures by pulling strings from above, unseen by the audience. The idiom was transferred from the arrangement of this show to politics. Whoever holds the strings is the one who decides unseen; the question ipler kimin elinde 'in whose hands are the strings' comes from the same image.

column2: To be a person without will who acts according to someone else's wishes.
column3: To be someone's puppet.
column4: A kukla is a figure of cloth and wood moved by strings or by hand; it cannot move on its own. Puppet shows appeared alongside Karagöz at Ottoman festivities. The idiom likens the puppet's lack of will to a person under someone else's control and is used especially in political criticism.

column2: To admit defeat; to give up.
column3: To say 'pes'.
column4: The Persian word pes means 'back, behind'; in wrestling and in fights the loser announced his surrender by saying pes. In Ottoman wrestling matches too, saying pes was the verbal acknowledgment of defeat. The idiom uses this word of surrender in the general sense of giving up; the form pes doğrusu, by contrast, expresses admiration.

column2: To come forward and begin to play an active role.
column3: To step onto the theater stage.
column4: Western-style theater spread in the Ottoman Empire in the 19th century with the Tanzimat reforms; the word sahne is of Arabic origin and acquired its theatrical meaning in this period. Sahneye çıkmak was used first of the actor and then of everyone who becomes visible in politics and public life. Sahneden çekilmek 'to withdraw from the stage' comes from the same image.

column2: To shy away from a struggle or a responsibility.
column3: To flee from the wrestling mat.
column4: In modern wrestling the bout takes place on a mat; a wrestler who leaves the mat to escape his opponent is penalized, and the behavior is considered cowardice. The idiom transferred the wrestling term to evasive behavior in politics and debate. Wrestling's status as the national sport in the Republican period made the idiom widespread.

column2: To roam about a place freely and at ease; to run riot.
column3: To play the game of jereed.
column4: Cirit (jereed) is an old Turkish game in which two teams on horseback hurl sticks at each other; it had a place in Ottoman court and military tradition, and Evliya Çelebi describes the jereed grounds. Riders playing jereed gallop across the field. The idiom likens this free galloping to roaming unchecked about a place, as in fareler cirit atıyor 'the mice are running riot'.

column2: To stall and postpone a problem instead of solving it.
column3: To kick the ball out over the touchline in football.
column4: In football a defender under pressure kicks the ball out over the touchline to gain time. Football entered Turkey at the end of the 19th century in Izmir and Istanbul and became the most widespread sport in the 20th century. The idiom passed from the language of football into politics and came to be used for administrators who put off a problem.

column2: To be deceived by falling for a trick.
column3: To fall into the game.
column4: Besides 'entertainment', the word oyun in Turkish also carries the sense of 'trick, ruse'; in the Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk the word oyun appears in both senses. In games such as backgammon and cards, someone who fell into a trap set by a cheating player was said to have oyuna geldi. The idiom preserves this sense; the form oyuna getirmek 'to trick someone' comes from the same root.

column2: To be a person without will of one's own, used in other people's plans.
column3: To be a pawn in chess.
column4: The pawn is the least valuable and most easily sacrificed piece in chess; the word entered Turkish via French pion. In the Ottoman chess tradition the same piece was called piyade 'foot soldier'. The idiom describes a person expended in the plans of the big players and is used especially in political writing; the form piyon gibi kullanmak 'to use like a pawn' is also common.

column2: Things that look attractive from a distance may not be so when seen up close.
column3: The sound of the drum is pleasant from afar.
column4: The drum is the instrument of weddings and holidays, of Ramadan nights and of the mehter band; from a distance its sound announces festivity, but standing next to it deafens the ears. Starting from this experience of sound, the proverb conveys that lives envied from afar look different up close. It comes from Ottoman festival culture.
